title: Who Had the Right?
description: The 1550 Valladolid debate: Sepúlveda's case for conquest, Las Casas's defense of Indigenous peoples, and the birth of the language of human rights.
essential_question: Could the conquest of the Americas be morally justified?
learning_objectives: Summarize Sepúlveda's argument from natural slavery and its Aristotelian roots.
Explain Las Casas's defense of Indigenous peoples, including his tragic early irony.
Evaluate why the debate changed little on the ground but mattered for the history of rights.

key_terms.definition: The 1550–51 council debate at Valladolid, Spain, over the justice of Spain's conquest of the Americas.
Sepúlveda's Aristotelian claim that some peoples are slaves by nature and may justly be ruled by force.
The idea first articulated at Valladolid that conquest itself can be judged by universal moral law.

narration.text: [solemn]Were the [es]conquistadors[/es] heroes or criminals? In 1550, Spain did something no empire had ever done: it put itself on trial. [beat] Before the emperor's council at [es]Valladolid[/es], two theologians debated whether Spain's wars in the Americas were just. The question on the table was not just about the past. It was about [emphasis]who had the right to rule[/emphasis].

scenes.production_notes: Cold open on the paradox; keep the portrait dim until the trial line lands.

narration.text: [fierce]Aristotle teaches that some peoples are slaves by nature, and that nature intends them to be ruled. War against such peoples is just when it brings them to Christianity and to civil order. [beat] Their rites are abominable. Their minds are unfit for self-rule. Conquest, therefore, [emphasis]needs no apology[/emphasis]. It is mercy in the shape of force.

scenes.production_notes: First-person debate voice. Sepulveda is cold and precise; let the logic sound airtight, then let Las Casas break it.

narration.text: [fierce]You call them natural slaves. I have lived among these peoples, and I tell you they are rational, capable of faith, and masters of their own lands by natural law. [beat] Your Aristotle never crossed the ocean. [pause:1] And I confess my own shame before you. I once urged African slaves to spare the Indians, a counsel I have [emphasis]spent my life denouncing[/emphasis].

narration.text: The debate changed almost nothing on the ground. The [es]encomienda[/es] and the slave trade continued. [beat] But [es]Valladolid[/es] invented something new: the idea that conquest itself could be judged by [emphasis]universal moral law[/emphasis]. That language, of natural rights and human dignity, would [slow]outlive the empire it failed to restrain[/slow].
